Floquet engineering of competing antiferromagnetism and
dd-wave superconductivity on the square lattice

Zhaoyu Han Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA 02138, USA    Subir Sachdev Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge MA 02138, USA
Abstract

We propose a driven Lieb–Hubbard quantum simulator whose prethermal dynamics realize a square-lattice spin-1/2 fermion model with independently tunable repulsive on-site and attractive bond interactions. Periodically modulating the charge-transfer offset between the site (dd) and bond (pp) orbitals of the Lieb lattice brings a pp-orbital doublon energetically close to a pair in the dd manifold while keeping all pp-orbital singlons off resonance, thereby creating a synthetic “negative-UU” center on a Lieb-lattice bond site. Two controlled eliminations then generate a compact bond attraction in the reduced dd-only model on the square lattice, despite the microscopic repulsion in the pp orbital. The resulting interaction JJ is tunable independently of the Hubbard repulsion UdU_{d} on the dd orbitals, while interference between photon-assisted paths provides access to an intermediate-coupling regime in which JJ and UdU_{d} are both comparable to the effective hopping. At half filling, a mean-field calculation in this regime finds adjacent antiferromagnetic and dd-wave superconducting phases, as well as narrow coexistence regions, suggesting close competition between these orders. We discuss the branch-preparation, prethermal, and higher-band conditions required to translate the formal construction into an optical-lattice protocol. More broadly, our work identifies a structural similarity between Floquet systems and electron–phonon problems that may guide the design of novel quantum-simulation protocols.

Introduction.— Ultracold fermions in optical lattices provide a highly controlled setting for quantum simulations of strongly correlated electronic systems. Rapid progress in this field [13, 16, 40, 20, 33], including significantly lowered effective temperatures and access to doped frustrated magnets [50], raises the prospect of studying the competition among orders relevant to the cuprates, such as dd-wave superconductivity (ddSC), antiferromagnetism (AF), and density-wave order. Their interplay remains a central puzzle in condensed-matter physics. The Hubbard model is a canonical arena for these phenomena [2] and has been extensively studied in optical-lattice platforms [13, 16, 40]. The status and scale of its putative ddSC phase nevertheless remain numerically delicate: the most controlled evidence is clearest at weak coupling, while the intermediate-coupling ground state remains under active debate [36, 47, 38]. This motivates a complementary perspective, particularly timely as quantum simulators acquire increasingly flexible controls, including Floquet driving [11, 35, 39, 46, 34, 45]: can one engineer a structured interaction that exposes the competition between AF and ddSC more directly?

This goal is not merely materials-specific; it also addresses fundamental questions in quantum many-body physics. The AF–ddSC boundary is a candidate setting for deconfined quantum criticality (DQCP) [48, 7, 8], whose existence and critical behavior remain under intense investigation. Recent sign-problem-free simulations of fermionic spinons and bosonic chargons coupled to a fluctuating SU(2) gauge field have found strong evidence for such a transition [6] at half filling.

Recent studies on electron–phonon models provide an important design lesson. Integrating out a fast phonon that modulates a lattice bond produces the square of a bond electronic operator in the effective electron-only model on the vertex lattice. Its decomposition can contain AF exchange, correlated hopping, and pair hopping, so the mediated coupling can promote both magnetic order and mobile Cooper pairing. This structure underlies the AF–ddSC competition in a bond-interaction model [3], in Su–Schrieffer–Heeger–Hubbard models [49, 5, 15, 51], and in a Lieb–Holstein model [18]. The same lesson appears in more microscopic studies of cuprates: a B1​gB_{1g} buckling phonon can enhance dd-wave pairing when AF and pairing tendencies are already close [23], consistent with the strongly anisotropic oxygen-mode vertices emphasized in Refs. [10, 26]. A real-space interpretation of these results is Anderson’s negative-UU-center mechanism [1]: a high-energy orbital that favors double occupation can lower the energy of an itinerant pair through virtual pair transfer even when that orbital is absent from the low-energy manifold. In the electron–phonon realizations, lattice vibration creates such attractive centers on bonds, and then a modest repulsive Hubbard interaction can suppress the competing on-site ss-wave channel and expose the bond-generated ddSC and AF tendencies. Recently, studies on similar e-ph models also found resonating-valence-bond (RVB) phases with emergent gauge structure [18, 4, 19], suggesting an emergent gauge theory description underlying the physics of such systems.

Our proposal asks whether a coherent Floquet drive can generate a similarly structured effective interaction. We begin with a Lieb–Hubbard model, a lattice geometry that has recently been realized in optical-lattice platforms [44, 31]. The construction is a driven negative-UU-center mechanism built from a nearly resonant bond-orbital doublon. Modulating the charge-transfer gap between the site (dd) and bond (pp) orbitals uses quasienergy periodicity to bring a one-photon replica of the pp doublon close to the dd-orbital branch, while the corresponding pp-singlon states remain off resonance [Fig. 1]. For positive dressed detuning, virtual occupation of this synthetic center lowers the energy of a dd-orbital pair and produces an interaction reminiscent of those generated by electron–phonon coupling on bonds. A mean-field calculation at half filling shows that the resulting dd-only model supports both ddSC and AF in its intermediate-coupling phase diagram.

This setup receives additional motivation from light-induced superconducting phenomena in the cuprates (or more generally phonon driven floquet matters [25]). Photoemission reveals a widespread 5050–8080 meV kink consistent with coupling to oxygen vibrations [30], while symmetry-resolved theory and experiment distinguish a predominantly antinodal B1​gB_{1g} buckling coupling from a more nodal bond-stretching coupling [10, 26, 37]. Resonant mid-infrared excitation of lattice modes in stripe-ordered and underdoped cuprates produces transient superconducting-like interlayer optical responses [14, 24], and time-resolved diffraction connects these responses to driven apical-oxygen and bond-buckling distortions [32]. If bond-buckling modes locally modulate the charge-transfer gap, the present cold-atom construction may provide a useful caricature of this mechanism.

The model.— We consider a Lieb–Hubbard model with a periodically driven charge-transfer gap,

H⁡(τ)=\displaystyle H(\tau)= −t∑⟨i​j⟩,σ[p⟨i​j⟩,σ†(di​σ+dj​σ)+h.c.]\displaystyle-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}\left[p^{\dagger}_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}(d_{i\sigma}+d_{j\sigma})+\mathrm{h.c.}\right]
+Up∑⟨i​j⟩np⟨i​j⟩,↑np⟨i​j⟩,↓+Ud∑indi↑ndi↓\displaystyle+U_{p}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}n^{p}_{\langle ij\rangle,\uparrow}n^{p}_{\langle ij\rangle,\downarrow}+U_{d}\sum_{i}n^{d}_{i\uparrow}n^{d}_{i\downarrow}
+[Δ+Acos(ωτ)]∑⟨i​j⟩n⟨i​j⟩p.\displaystyle+[\Delta+A\cos(\omega\tau)]\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}n^{p}_{\langle ij\rangle}. (1)

Here di​σd_{i\sigma} annihilates a fermion on a square-lattice vertex and p⟨i​j⟩,σp_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma} annihilates one at a nearest-neighbor bond center. We take both UdU_{d} and UpU_{p} to be repulsive, as is natural for two hyperfine states with a positive scattering length. The reference filling is one fermion per unit cell. We assume

t,Ud≪Δ,Up,ℏ​ω≃2​Δ+Up,t,\ U_{d}\ll\Delta,U_{p},\qquad\hbar\omega\simeq 2\Delta+U_{p}, (2)

so that all one-particle and spatially separated two-particle pp excitations remain off resonance. The drive amplitude must also remain below the gap to unwanted Wannier bands. These assumptions are stated quantitatively in the End Matter.

Floquet–boson correspondence.— The analogy between the Floquet problem and an electron–boson problem, such as an electron–phonon model, becomes explicit in the rotating frame. With n^p=∑⟨i​j⟩n⟨i​j⟩p\hat{n}_{p}=\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}n^{p}_{\langle ij\rangle} and κ=A/(ℏ​ω)\kappa=A/(\hbar\omega), the transformation W⁡(τ)=exp⁡[−i​κ​sin⁡(ω​τ)​n^p]W(\tau)=\exp[-i\kappa\sin(\omega\tau)\hat{n}_{p}] removes the modulation and changes the hybridization to

−t∑⟨i​j⟩,σ[ei​κ​sin⁡(ω​τ)p⟨i​j⟩,σ†(di​σ+dj​σ)+h.c.].-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}\left[e^{i\kappa\sin(\omega\tau)}p^{\dagger}_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}(d_{i\sigma}+d_{j\sigma})+\mathrm{h.c.}\right]. (3)

The phase has the Jacobi–Anger expansion

ei​κ​sin⁡ω​τ=∑m=−∞∞𝒥m​(κ)​ei​m​ω​τ,e^{i\kappa\sin\omega\tau}=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}{\cal J}_{m}(\kappa)e^{im\omega\tau}, (4)

where 𝒥m{\cal J}_{m} is the Bessel function of the first kind. In Holstein-type electron-phonon models, a Lang–Firsov transformation similarly dresses electron hopping with a phonon displacement operator, whose matrix elements generate Franck–Condon sidebands and integer-shifted virtual denominators [29, 17, 18]. In Sambe space, mm labels a synthetic ladder of photon replicas, and the Bessel amplitudes are the coherent-drive analogues of Franck–Condon weights. Unlike a zero-temperature phonon vacuum, however, a classical drive supplies and absorbs quanta symmetrically. It can therefore place a selected composite excitation at a small, sign-tunable quasienergy detuning. The drive thus creates a branch-selective resonant channel rather than simply reproducing a phonon-mediated attraction. We emphasize, however, that a classical drive generates neither a phonon cloud nor the associated polaronic dressing. In particular, interference among drive-assisted virtual processes permits the magnitudes, signs, and relative weights of the mediated hopping and interaction terms to be tuned more flexibly than in conventional electron–phonon settings.

The perturbation theory.— Under the assumed hierarchy of scales, high-energy states can be eliminated through two successive Schrieffer–Wolff transformations. The first step removes singly occupied pp orbitals while retaining the nearly resonant pp doublon. For convenience, we define the bonding orbital of two neighboring sites d[i+j]≡(di+dj)/2d_{[i+j]}\equiv(d_{i}+d_{j})/\sqrt{2} and

D[i+j]†\displaystyle D^{\dagger}_{[i+j]} =d[i+j]↑†​d[i+j]↓†,\displaystyle=d^{\dagger}_{[i+j]\uparrow}d^{\dagger}_{[i+j]\downarrow}, (5)
P⟨i​j⟩†\displaystyle P^{\dagger}_{\langle ij\rangle} =p⟨i​j⟩,↑†​p⟨i​j⟩,↓†.\displaystyle=p^{\dagger}_{\langle ij\rangle,\uparrow}p^{\dagger}_{\langle ij\rangle,\downarrow}. (6)

Here D[i+j]†D^{\dagger}_{[i+j]} creates a pair in the dd bonding orbital; we call it a dd-bond pair. P⟨i​j⟩†P^{\dagger}_{\langle ij\rangle} creates two fermions on the single bond-center pp orbital; we call this hard-core boson a PP dimer. Second-order virtual processes produce nearest-neighbor hopping within the dd manifold, coherent DD-PP pair conversion and Lamb shift of detuning:

teff\displaystyle t_{\rm eff} =t2Δ​𝒯,Λ=2​t2Δ​ℒ,\displaystyle=\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta}{\cal T}\ ,\quad\quad\Lambda=\frac{2t^{2}}{\Delta}{\cal L}, (7)
δR\displaystyle\delta_{R} =2​Δ+Up−ℏ​ω+4​t2Δ​(ℛ+𝒯)\displaystyle=2\Delta+U_{p}-\hbar\omega+\frac{4t^{2}}{\Delta}({\cal R}+{\cal T}) (8)

where we define dimensionless coefficients

𝒯\displaystyle{\cal T} =∑m𝒥m​(κ)21−m​ℏ​ω/Δ,\displaystyle=\sum_{m}\frac{{\cal J}_{m}(\kappa)^{2}}{1-m\hbar\omega/\Delta}, (9)
ℒ\displaystyle{\cal L} =∑m𝒥m(κ)𝒥1−m(κ)[−Up/Δ+(1−2m)ℏω/Δ](1−m​ℏ​ω/Δ)​[1+Up/Δ−(1−m)​ℏ​ω/Δ]\displaystyle=\sum_{m}\frac{{\cal J}_{m}(\kappa){\cal J}_{1-m}(\kappa)[-U_{p}/\Delta+(1-2m)\hbar\omega/\Delta]}{(1-m\hbar\omega/\Delta)[1+U_{p}/\Delta-(1-m)\hbar\omega/\Delta]} (10)
ℛ\displaystyle{\cal R} =∑m𝒥m​(κ)21+Up/Δ−m​ℏ​ω/Δ.\displaystyle=\sum_{m}\frac{{\cal J}_{m}(\kappa)^{2}}{1+U_{p}/\Delta-m\hbar\omega/\Delta}. (11)

Because these processes can be Pauli blocked, they also generate an interaction between the dd fermions and the PP dimers. After the uniform Lamb shift has been absorbed into δR\delta_{R}, the remaining interaction term is

HP​d=\displaystyle H_{Pd}={} 2​t2Δ​(𝒯−ℛ)​∑⟨i​j⟩P⟨i​j⟩†​P⟨i​j⟩​n[i+j].\displaystyle\frac{2t^{2}}{\Delta}({\cal T}-{\cal R})\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}P_{\langle ij\rangle}^{\dagger}P_{\langle ij\rangle}n_{[i+j]}. (12)

Collecting these terms, the first elimination gives, to leading order in t/Δt/\Delta and Ud/ΔU_{d}/\Delta,

Hmd=\displaystyle H_{\rm md}={} Hd+δR​∑⟨i​j⟩P⟨i​j⟩†​P⟨i​j⟩\displaystyle H_{d}+\delta_{R}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}P_{\langle ij\rangle}^{\dagger}P_{\langle ij\rangle}
+Λ∑⟨i​j⟩(P⟨i​j⟩†D[i+j]+h.c.)+HP​d,\displaystyle+\Lambda\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}(P_{\langle ij\rangle}^{\dagger}D_{[i+j]}+\mathrm{h.c.})+H_{Pd}, (13)

where HdH_{d} is the square-lattice Hubbard Hamiltonian

Hd=\displaystyle H_{d}={} −teff∑⟨i​j⟩,σ(di​σ†dj​σ+h.c.)+Ud∑ini↑dni↓d.\displaystyle-t_{\rm eff}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}(d^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}d_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.})+U_{d}\sum_{i}n^{d}_{i\uparrow}n^{d}_{i\downarrow}. (14)

This is a two-channel lattice Feshbach model and must be retained whenever |δR||\delta_{R}| is comparable to the pair-conversion amplitude, the dd-bandwidth, or the blocking interaction, which are all 𝒪⁡(t2/Δ)\mathcal{O}(t^{2}/\Delta).

For a moderately large positive dressed detuning,

Δ≫δR≫t2/Δ,\Delta\gg\delta_{R}\gg t^{2}/\Delta, (15)

the PP-dimer states lie at higher energy and can be eliminated in a second-stage expansion, in which case HP​dH_{Pd} is no longer important. This gives a dd-only effective model on the vertex square lattice:

H□\displaystyle H_{\square} =Hd−2​J​∑⟨i​j⟩D[i+j]†​D[i+j],\displaystyle=H_{d}-2J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}D^{\dagger}_{[i+j]}D_{[i+j]}, (16)

where J=|Λ|2/(2​δR)>0J=|\Lambda|^{2}/(2\delta_{R})>0. Nonresonant fourth-order corrections are O⁡(t4/Δ3)O(t^{4}/\Delta^{3}) and thus subleading in the assumed hierarchy of scales. The bond operator with strength JJ contains an AF exchange +J𝑺i⋅𝑺j+J\,\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}, density and correlated-hopping interactions, and pair hopping (End Matter). Decomposed in the Cooper channel, it induces attraction in both the dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}}-wave and ss-wave channels. The Hubbard repulsion UdU_{d} penalizes the on-site component of the ss-wave channel and thereby exposes the dd-wave pairing channel, allowing Ud/JU_{d}/J to tune between ss and dd pairing.

The models in Eqs. (13) and (16) are structurally identical to effective models descending from the Lieb–Holstein model [18]. Reference [18] also identifies a controlled route to a quantum dimer model, and hence to RVB physics, when the PP dimers lie below the dd manifold. This corresponds here to a negative detuning, δR<0\delta_{R}<0. Such a regime is in principle accessible in the present setup, but it requires preparing a distinct prethermal branch with a substantial initial population of PP dimers. The dimer-monomer model in Eq. 13 is also similar to what was used to realize spin liquid states in a Bosonic Lieb-Hubbard setup [27].

Controlling the coupling strength.— We aim to simulate the intermediate-coupling regime of Eq. (16), where competing orders can emerge at intermediate temperature scales. At first sight, the effective model seems incompatible with this goal. For a generic drive amplitude, tefft_{\rm eff} and Λ\Lambda are both O⁡(t2/Δ)O(t^{2}/\Delta), suggesting

J|teff|\displaystyle\frac{J}{|t_{\rm eff}|} =|Λ|2​|teff|​|Λ|δR∼?|Λ|δR≪1\displaystyle=\frac{|\Lambda|}{2|t_{\rm eff}|}\frac{|\Lambda|}{\delta_{R}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{\sim}}\frac{|\Lambda|}{\delta_{R}}\ll 1 (17)

in the controlled second-elimination limit. The additional control provided by κ\kappa, however, allows J/|teff|∼1J/|t_{\rm eff}|\sim 1 while preserving the perturbative hierarchy. The key observation is that the all-harmonic sum for tefft_{\rm eff} has interference zeros at which Λ\Lambda remains nonzero. Let κ∗\kappa_{*} denote such a zero. Choosing κ\kappa close, but not equal, to κ∗\kappa_{*} can enhance |Λ|/(2​|teff|)|\Lambda|/(2|t_{\rm eff}|) enough to compensate for the small ratio |Λ|/δR|\Lambda|/\delta_{R}. This provides access to the intermediate-coupling regime

|teff|∼J∼Ud.\displaystyle|t_{\rm eff}|\sim J\sim U_{d}. (18)

Figure 2 illustrates this lever using the complete harmonic sums: the ratio J/|teff|J/|t_{\text{eff}}| can indeed be tuned by κ\kappa in a wide range while keeping the control parameters small. A caveat, though, is that this tuning also suppresses the overall energy scale of the effective model. An experiment must therefore choose a finite compromise between interaction-to-hopping ratio, absolute temperature scale, and lifetime.

Mean-field calculation.— To test the tendencies toward ddSC and AF in the square-lattice model, Eq. (16), we solve the saddle point equations for multiple orders at zero temperature, and audit the results with unbiased Gaussian states using a repeated 2×22\times 2 supercell. All particle–hole and particle–particle bilinears allowed within this cell, together with their arbitrary coexistence, are treated on an equal footing. The End Matter gives further details of the calculation. Figure 3 summarizes the resulting phase diagram, which contains regimes of ssSC, ddSC, AF, and coexistence.

These mean-field results are not controlled at intermediate coupling and should therefore be regarded as suggestive. It is nevertheless notable that the phase diagram is qualitatively consistent with beyond-mean-field studies of closely related models descending from electron–phonon problems. Assaad’s quantum Monte Carlo study of a bond-hopping-square interaction found a half-filled evolution from ddSC to AF as the repulsion increases [3]. Sign-problem-free simulations show that bond SSH phonons generate AF exchange and order [5], while DMRG finds robust ddSC upon doping from the combined SSH coupling and Hubbard repulsion, between AF and ssSC regimes [49]. This agreement across related models and independent methods makes the competing tendencies plausible, while leaving their precise boundaries and transition structure as strongly correlated many-body questions for the Floquet simulator.

Preparation and limitations.— Quasienergies are periodic modulo ℏ​ω\hbar\omega, so an exact Floquet spectrum has no canonical ground state [22]. Here “ground state” means the low-entropy state of the branch-selected prethermal Hamiltonian. At zero drive the conversion Λ\Lambda vanishes, while the positive charge-transfer gap makes the cooled gas dd-orbital dominated. For δR>0\delta_{R}>0—a red-detuned drive—this initial state connects continuously to the lower, dd-like branch of the resonant pair-dimer block. The modulation should be ramped while the dressed mediator energy remains positive, with the frequency adjusted if necessary to compensate its amplitude-dependent Lamb shift. The observation window must satisfy

τramp,ℏ/J≪τheat.\tau_{\rm ramp},\ \hbar/J\ll\tau_{\rm heat}. (19)

Several experimental risks are independent and should not be hidden by the formal scaling limit. First, unwanted one-particle, separated-pair, and many-body resonances must remain outside the effective bandwidth. Second, the required modulation amplitude can couple to higher Wannier bands even when the tight-binding derivation remains controlled. Third, real pp-doublon population, spatially varying Lamb shifts, and interaction-dependent detuning can broaden the resonance. All these factors require a careful assessment for a specific experimental implementation.

Discussion and outlook.— Our work establishes a controlled route from repulsive microscopic interactions to a structured attraction with flexibly tunable strength. This setup may expose the competition between AF and ddSC directly in a quantum simulator. Our approach is complementary to the route studied in Ref. [21], where circular light driving modifies photoassisted hopping, the Fermi surface, and the magnetic fluctuation spectrum; within Floquet random-phase approximation (RPA), d+i​dd+id pairing appears near the AF boundary and evolves toward triplet pp-wave pairing near a Floquet Lifshitz transition. The drive there acts primarily through the one-particle dispersion, so the pairing kernel is inherited indirectly from the driven magnetic fluctuations and is tied to the accompanying band reconstruction. Our construction instead focuses on engineering the effective interactions. Related works also explored schemes suppressing hopping relative to superexchange in the large-UU limit [9]; near half filling, however, this hierarchy freezes charge dynamics and may not lead to ddSC [12, 17].

Conceptually, our work also develops an intimate connection between Floquet and electron–boson problems. We expect this bridge to provide further design principles for driven quantum matter. For example, the same kind of bond electron-phonon models have been argued to host high-temperature SC [43, 52, 28, 49] away from half-filling. This physics may be studied in the current setup in an analog way.

Appendix A End Matter

A.1 Details of the virtual processes

In rotating frame formulation of the problem, provided that none of the appreciably weighted singly occupied pp states is resonant, this sector can be eliminated perturbatively. The resulting second-order processes generate the effective hopping tefft_{\rm eff}, the pair-conversion amplitude Λ\Lambda, and the diagonal shifts entering δR\delta_{R} and HP​dH_{Pd}, as given in the main text. The effective hopping arises when a fermion initially on a dd orbital virtually enters the intervening pp orbital and subsequently exits onto the neighboring dd orbital. Because the initial and final states belong to the same Floquet replica, the two hops carry the harmonic weight 𝒥m​(κ)2{\cal J}_{m}(\kappa)^{2} and the intermediate singlon has energy denominator Δ−m​ℏ​ω\Delta-m\hbar\omega. Pair conversion instead involves two fermions from the symmetric dd-bond orbital successively entering the same pp orbital. The two hops together transfer one drive quantum, which can be partitioned between them as mm and 1−m1-m; the corresponding paths therefore interfere with weights 𝒥m​(κ)​𝒥1−m​(κ){\cal J}_{m}(\kappa){\cal J}_{1-m}(\kappa). Since the initial dd-bond pair and final PP dimer are not exactly degenerate, the Hermitian second-order matrix element contains denominators referenced to both endpoint energies, as retained in the expression for Λ\Lambda in the main text. The enhanced hybridization of the normalized symmetric dd-bond orbital and the two spin orderings account for its overall prefactor. The remaining second-order processes are diagonal. When the bond-center pp orbital is empty, a fermion can execute the sequence d→p→dd\rightarrow p\rightarrow d, producing the ordinary dd-sector renormalization and the shift of a dd-bond pair. When the pp orbital contains a PP dimer, the allowed sequence is instead p→d→pp\rightarrow d\rightarrow p, which produces the dimer Lamb shift. The difference between these shifts renormalizes the pair-transfer detuning from δ\delta to δR\delta_{R}. Their dependence on the occupations of both orbitals also leaves the operator-valued blocking term HP​dH_{Pd}: a PP dimer removes the d→p→dd\rightarrow p\rightarrow d path, while occupation of dd Pauli-blocks the reverse p→d→pp\rightarrow d\rightarrow p process.

A.2 Effective interaction content

The compact bond attraction can be decomposed as

−2J∑⟨i​j⟩D[i+j]†D[i+j]\displaystyle-2J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}D_{[i+j]}^{\dagger}D_{[i+j]}
=\displaystyle={} −2J∑ini↑ni↓−J4∑⟨i​j⟩ninj+J∑⟨i​j⟩𝑺i⋅𝑺j\displaystyle-2J\sum_{i}n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}-\frac{J}{4}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}n_{i}n_{j}+J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\bm{S}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{j}
−J2∑⟨i​j⟩,σBi​j,σ(ni​σ¯+nj​σ¯)−J2∑⟨i​j⟩(di↑†di↓†dj↓dj↑+h.c.).\displaystyle-\frac{J}{2}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}B_{ij,\sigma}(n_{i\bar{\sigma}}+n_{j\bar{\sigma}})-\frac{J}{2}\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left(d^{\dagger}_{i\uparrow}d^{\dagger}_{i\downarrow}d_{j\downarrow}d_{j\uparrow}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right). (E1)

where Bi​j,σ=di​σ†​dj​σ+h.c.B_{ij,\sigma}=d^{\dagger}_{i\sigma}d_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{h.c.} is the hopping operator. This coupling therefore generates an antiferromagnetic exchange, reduces the net local repulsion to Ud−2​JU_{d}-2J, and produces nearest-neighbor density, correlated-hopping, and pair-hopping interactions.

At zero center-of-mass momentum, the pairing kernel generated by the compact interaction is

V(𝒌,𝒌′)=−2J∑α=x,y(1+coskα)(1+coskα′).V(\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime})=-2J\sum_{\alpha=x,y}(1+\cos k_{\alpha})(1+\cos k^{\prime}_{\alpha}). (E2)

Introducing the A1​gA_{1g} and B1​gB_{1g} form factors

fs​(𝒌)=2+cos⁡kx+cos⁡ky,fd​(𝒌)=cos⁡kx−cos⁡ky,f_{s}(\bm{k})=2+\cos k_{x}+\cos k_{y},\qquad f_{d}(\bm{k})=\cos k_{x}-\cos k_{y}, (E3)

the kernel separates exactly as

V⁡(𝒌,𝒌′)=−J​fs​(𝒌)​fs​(𝒌′)−J​fd​(𝒌)​fd​(𝒌′).V(\bm{k},\bm{k}^{\prime})=-Jf_{s}(\bm{k})f_{s}(\bm{k}^{\prime})-Jf_{d}(\bm{k})f_{d}(\bm{k}^{\prime}). (E4)

The first term belongs to the fully symmetric A1​gA_{1g} sector and contains both on-site and extended-ss components. The second is a pure B1​gB_{1g} or dx2−y2d_{x^{2}-y^{2}} channel.

A.3 Numerical method

We determine the zero-temperature phase diagram of Eq. (16) at half filling, setting teff=1t_{\rm eff}=1. The quantitative phase boundaries are obtained from a symmetry-adapted Gaussian calculation that retains the five candidate saddles found in the scan: ssSC, s+i​ds+id, ddSC, AF+ddSC, and AF. For each J/teff=0,0.0125,…,0.5J/t_{\rm eff}=0,0.0125,\ldots,0.5, we construct the corresponding Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonian from the normal bond expectation values, staggered magnetization, on-site anomalous average, and complex nearest-neighbor singlet amplitudes. The resulting fixed-point equations are solved to determine the ground state. We use logarithmic variables for small order parameters, continuation from neighboring parameter points, and multiple initial seeds. The lowest energy per site among the converged saddles is selected.

The boundaries are refined directly rather than read from a finite grid in UdU_{d}. The ssSC–s+i​ds+id and s+i​ds+id–ddSC boundaries are located where the linearized subdominant pairing eigenvalue in the corresponding self-consistent superconducting background reaches unity. Similarly, the two edges of the AF+ddSC region are obtained from the AF instability of the ddSC saddle and the dd-wave instability of the AF saddle. If two locally stable saddles compete before either loses stability, we instead locate the zero of their energy difference. At small JJ, the superconducting gaps and the s+i​ds+id coexistence window become exponentially small; when that window cannot be resolved nonlinearly, we report the crossing of the linearized ss- and dd-wave gap scales and set its displayed width to zero. The Brillouin-zone integrals use an infrared-adapted quadrature with logarithmically spaced panels resolving both the Fermi surface and the half-filled van Hove points. Increasing the outer quadrature from 32 to 64 nodes and the infrared resolution from 14 to 18 decades shifts the reported boundaries by less than 1.5×10−3​teff1.5\times 10^{-3}t_{\rm eff}. As a separate benchmark, the J=0J=0 calculation recovers the nested Hubbard result: every Ud>0U_{d}>0 has an AF saddle below the normal state.

We then audit, rather than determine, these boundaries with an unrestricted periodically repeated 2×22\times 2 supercell. For each of the four site orbitals and eight positively oriented nearest-neighbor bonding orbitals, this calculation retains the complete spin-resolved 2×22\times 2 normal density matrix and the complex same-orbital singlet anomalous density. These are all normal and anomalous self-energies generated by the Gaussian variational derivative of the original compact interaction, without imposing phase labels before convergence. Together with the chemical potential, the stationary problem contains 73 real variables and a 16×1616\times 16 Bogoliubov–de Gennes Hamiltonian. We first performed a coarse unrestricted scan on a 6×166\times 16 grid covering 0≤J/teff≤0.50\leq J/t_{\rm eff}\leq 0.5 and 0≤Ud/teff≤1.50\leq U_{d}/t_{\rm eff}\leq 1.5. We then carried out 114 higher-resolution optimizations at the 19 parameter points marked by open circles in Fig. 3, using six starts per point: the symmetry-adapted solution and charge-density-wave, valence-bond, nematic, pair-density-wave, and random mixed textures. All runs converged with residuals below 2.0×10−72.0\times 10^{-7}; no lower-energy translation-breaking solution was found, and independently converged energies agreed within 4.2×10−9​teff4.2\times 10^{-9}t_{\rm eff} per site. These audits substantially reduce initialization and supercell bias but do not exclude disconnected minima, incommensurate order, periods longer than 2×22\times 2, or phase separation.

A.4 Branch selection and operational ground state

The local pair-conversion problem is described by

Hloc=(0Λ∗ΛδR),E±=δR±δR2+4​|Λ|22.H_{\rm loc}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\Lambda^{*}\\ \Lambda&\delta_{R}\end{pmatrix},\qquad E_{\pm}=\frac{\delta_{R}\pm\sqrt{\delta_{R}^{2}+4|\Lambda|^{2}}}{2}. (E5)

For δR>0\delta_{R}>0, the lower eigenstate E−E_{-} is predominantly a dd-bond pair and is shifted downward by −|Λ|2/δR-|\Lambda|^{2}/\delta_{R}. This produces the attractive interaction and corresponds to a red-detuned drive. For δR<0\delta_{R}<0, the PP dimer instead forms the lower branch; the dd-like state is E+E_{+} and is shifted upward by +|Λ|2/|δR|+|\Lambda|^{2}/|\delta_{R}|. Shifting either quasienergy by an integer multiple of ℏ​ω\hbar\omega changes its representative in the Floquet zone but not its orbital composition or its connection to the initial state.

With the modulation switched off, Λ=0\Lambda=0, and the large positive charge-transfer gap makes the cooled system predominantly dd-orbital in character. The proposed protocol ramps the drive from this state while keeping δR>0\delta_{R}>0, so that the prepared state remains connected to the lower, dd-like branch. For a ramp dominated by the variation of Λ\Lambda at approximately fixed δR\delta_{R}, the local adiabaticity and prethermal conditions are

ℏ​|Λ˙|δR2≪1,τramp≪τheat.\frac{\hbar|\dot{\Lambda}|}{\delta_{R}^{2}}\ll 1,\qquad\tau_{\rm ramp}\ll\tau_{\rm heat}. (E6)

One must additionally impose adiabaticity relative to any many-body gap possessed by the target state. In a gapless thermodynamic phase, the operational objective is instead to preserve a sufficiently low entropy during the ramp. Floquet–Gibbs cooling is not generic because an external bath may exchange both energy and drive quanta with the system [42, 41]. The relevant notion of a ground state is therefore the low-entropy state of a branch-selected prethermal Hamiltonian, not the state of lowest exact quasienergy.

A.5 Validity conditions

In addition to t/Δ≪1t/\Delta\ll 1, the construction implicitly requires the following conditions:

  1. 1.

    For every appreciably weighted harmonic, the singlon denominators |Δ−m​ℏ​ω||\Delta-m\hbar\omega| and |Δ+Up−m​ℏ​ω||\Delta+U_{p}-m\hbar\omega| must remain large compared with the corresponding Bessel-weighted tunneling matrix elements and the relevant low-energy bandwidths.

  2. 2.

    The separated-particle detuning |2​Δ−ℏ​ω|=|Up−δ||2\Delta-\hbar\omega|=|U_{p}-\delta| must exceed the effective two-particle bandwidth, so that the drive selectively addresses the on-orbital PP dimer rather than two spatially separated pp fermions.

  3. 3.

    The retained energy scales must satisfy Ud,|teff|,J≪ℏ​ωU_{d},|t_{\rm eff}|,J\ll\hbar\omega, and no combination resonance involving UdU_{d} may fall inside the prethermal bandwidth.

  4. 4.

    Both the modulation amplitude A=κ​ℏ​ωA=\kappa\hbar\omega and the drive frequency must remain below the relevant gaps to unwanted Wannier bands.

  5. 5.

    The heating time must satisfy τheat≫τramp,ℏ/J\tau_{\rm heat}\gg\tau_{\rm ramp},\hbar/J.

The first three conditions isolate the desired Sambe crossing and justify the effective low-energy description. The fourth protects the assumed orbital Hilbert space, while the fifth is a dynamical requirement rather than a property of the Schrieffer–Wolff expansion. Satisfying all these conditions while retaining a useful absolute value of JJ is the central practical challenge of the proposal.
